summary:
Yobe State stands under the framework of Nigeria. Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the statute reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed; Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live under proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by these sources.

Entry itself carries criminal exposure. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression in Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025, updated April 2026) records that the federal criminal code penalises same-sex male conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment and three years for attempts, and is silent on women. The Sharia penal codes of the twelve northern states apply to Muslims, with death the maximum for men in all twelve and penalties for acts between women ranging from death in a minority of those states to flogging and imprisonment.

Yobe is one of those twelve states and carries the full weight of that layer. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Yobe among the twelve states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, the only states whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law. Shari'a was established in Yobe in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim, and the state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims. A Muslim visitor in Yobe therefore faces a parallel criminal jurisdiction in which male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death.

The enforcement texture matters more than the statute book. The UK Home Office note's enforcement and Hisbah section records the public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023, and notes that few secular cases reach court. Punishment for gender expression in Yobe is more likely to arrive as corporal punishment administered outside a courtroom than as a prosecution under the SSMPA.

There are no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people in Nigeria, and violence risk is documented. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Trans people face documented killing with no resulting prosecution. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged. Police extortion keyed to perceived sexuality is also documented: TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.
tangentialFactors:
The twelve northern states are not uniform in how the Shari'a penal codes treat women. The UK Home Office note records that penalties for acts between women range from death in a minority of those states to flogging and imprisonment elsewhere, while the federal criminal code is silent on women altogether. Which of those scales applies inside Yobe specifically is not set out in the sources available here.

The gap between formal penalty and actual exposure runs in both directions. The note observes that few secular cases reach court, which lowers the likelihood of a full SSMPA prosecution while leaving the extrajudicial layer intact, including the recorded public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023 and the pattern of police demands for money.

The one trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerned offences unrelated to identity. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion.

An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations in that case but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender. The finding concerns conditions of confinement, not the lawfulness of the sentence.
localsOnly:
Residents of Yobe have lived under a parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction since 2000, when Shari'a was established in the state under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report identifies Yobe as one of twelve states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, and the only category of state whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law. The state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims, which determines who is drawn into that jurisdiction.

For Muslim residents the practical consequence is exposure to penalties that federal law does not carry. The UK Home Office note records death as the maximum for men in all twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes, with women's conduct punished from death in a minority of those states to flogging and imprisonment. Local enforcement machinery includes Hisbah bodies, and the same note records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023.

Corrections placement for trans detainees is governed by the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, and an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing Bobrisky in a maximum-security prison breached that Act for a first-time offender. The panel's report addressed conditions of custody rather than the sentence itself; she had pleaded guilty on 5 April 2024 to four counts of naira abuse, received the maximum six months without a fine option on 12 April 2024, and was released on 5 August 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is unsettled by the sources here; the current summary treats them as proposals, not law.

The sources establish that Yobe adopted Shari'a into its criminal legislation but do not reproduce Yobe's own penal code text. The specific Zina provisions and the precise scale of penalties for acts between women as applied in Yobe, as distinct from the range across the twelve northern states, are not sourced here.

No case in this inventory records a foreign trans visitor prosecuted in Yobe. The trans-specific imprisonment case concerns naira abuse, and the documented violence cases are located in Abuja and Lagos.

Whether entry screening, identification checks or device and dating-app inspection are applied to arriving travellers in Yobe is not sourced. The kito-gang reporting concerns luring through apps after arrival rather than border procedure.

The 2026 travel warning is available here as reported by Sahara Reporters rather than read from the primary UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office text, so its wording should be treated as second-hand.
